RangeGuide.title: What is a poker range
RangeGuide.intro: A range isn't one hand - it's the whole set of hands a player could hold given a specific action in a specific spot. When someone says "they open wide", they don't mean one hand, they mean dozens of possible ones - some they'll continue with, some they'll fold.
RangeGuide.whyTitle: Why think in ranges at all
RangeGuide.whyBody: You never see your opponent's cards before showdown - only their actions: raise, call, fold. An action narrows down the hands they could be playing that way. That's range reading: not "they probably have AK", but "this action fits about twenty percent of their hands, and here's roughly which ones".
RangeGuide.gridTitle: What a range looks like: the 13x13 grid
RangeGuide.gridIntro: Every starting hand in hold'em fits a 13x13 grid - 169 cells, one per rank combination. A range is just a shaded part of that grid. Below is a real opening chart by position (the same one used in Whygrid reviews) - pick a position and see the width change.
RangeGuide.tightWideTitle: Tight and wide ranges, in numbers
RangeGuide.tightWideBody: "Tight" and "wide" aren't a gut call - they're a share of all 1326 possible hand combinations. Opening from UTG (the earliest seat) is roughly {utg}% of hands: nobody's folded yet, so you play carefully. Opening from the BTN (the last seat before the blinds) is roughly {btn}%: everyone else has already folded, so you can play noticeably wider.
RangeGuide.inProductBody: During a review the coach sometimes asks: "what range did you put your opponent on before the money went in?" You answer on the same grid, not in text - you click the hands you think they had. From there the coach isn't guessing equity in words - the algorithm computes the exact number against the hands you marked. You call the range, the code does the math.
RangeGuide.chartsLinkText: All of Whygrid's ranges - opens, BB defense, 3-bet, push-fold - live on the charts page
RangeGuide.ctaNote: Want to see what your opponent's range looks like inside a review of your own tournament? The first review is free.

PushFoldGuide.title: Push-fold chart - when to shove short-stacked
PushFoldGuide.intro: Once your stack drops under 15 big blinds, your first move into the pot usually isn't a sized raise - it's straight to all-in or fold: there's barely anything left to play post-flop, so splitting the bet doesn't make sense. That's push-fold - one decision, no streets after it. Below is a reference chart for which hands to shove first into the pot, by position and stack depth.
PushFoldGuide.whenBody: When everyone's folded to you and your stack is 0 to 14 big blinds. Deeper than 15 BB it's a regular open-raise instead - that's a separate "opening" chart. HJ plays the same column as CO here - there's no separate one for it.
PushFoldGuide.numbersBody: At 10 BB or less (the short band), shoving from UTG covers roughly {utg}% of hands, while from the BTN it's already about {btn}%: the later your seat, the less reason to wait for a stronger hand - almost no one's left to act behind you.
PushFoldGuide.inProductBody: When you shove all-in first into the pot on a short stack, the coach checks your hand against this exact chart - not a gut call. If the shove is noticeably wider than the norm, the coach asks why you picked that hand instead of just calling it a mistake outright.
PushFoldGuide.chartsLinkText: The rest of the charts - opens, BB defense, 3-bet, calling a shove - live on the charts page
PushFoldGuide.icmLinkText: A short stack near the money is an ICM question too, not just push width. See -
PushFoldGuide.ctaNote: Want to find out where your real shoves run wider than the norm? The first tournament review is free.

HandReviewGuide.title: How a poker hand review actually works
HandReviewGuide.intro: Replaying a hand yourself - opening the history, trying to remember what happened - almost always ends at "eh, seemed fine" or "ugh, just bad luck". A real review starts with exact numbers for every decision, not a feeling in hindsight, and someone asking why you did what you did - not just calling it wrong.
HandReviewGuide.numbersBody: A hand-history file is an exact record: who bet how much and when, which cards showed up. From it you can compute, not estimate: how often you enter a pot voluntarily, how many chips a specific decision cost you, what the pot odds were at the moment you called, what your hand's equity was against the villain's range. We do this with a precise algorithm, not the coach and not a language model: the numbers come out the same every run, they're never just a "feeling".
HandReviewGuide.exampleVpipDesc: How often you voluntarily enter a pot pre-flop - by calling or raising. High means you're playing lots of hands, low means you're tight.
HandReviewGuide.examplePotOddsDesc: How much you need to put in relative to what's already in the pot - compared against your chance to improve, to see if calling pays off.
HandReviewGuide.exampleEquityDesc: Your share of the pot right now - the percentage chance you win the hand against a villain's hand or range.
HandReviewGuide.questionsTitle: Then, questions - not a ready-made verdict
HandReviewGuide.questionsBody: The coach doesn't open with "you were wrong, here's the right answer". First it asks: what range did you put your opponent on, why that bet size, what were you thinking at the moment of the decision. Only after your answer - checked against the numbers, not a guess - does it say what actually happened. The difference is you arrive at the conclusion yourself, on your own numbers, instead of memorizing someone else's ready answer that fades by the next hand.
HandReviewGuide.notSolverDesc: The coach doesn't hand you a "GTO-correct" answer down to the percent - it checks your hand against reference charts and explains the gap. There's no single correct range - this is our own agreed baseline, not an absolute.
HandReviewGuide.notRtaDesc: A review is always about hands already played, after the tournament - never advice during play. Real-time assistance (RTA) is banned on most rooms - Whygrid never touches a live hand.
HandReviewGuide.notPromiseDesc: A review finds the decisions that repeat and cost you money over the long run. Fixing a leak isn't a guarantee you'll win any given tournament - poker stays a game with variance.

IcmGuide.title: What is ICM in poker tournaments
IcmGuide.intro: In a cash game, a chip is worth a chip. In a tournament it isn't - you can't cash out your stack at face value, you only have a shot at reaching the payouts and getting your share. ICM (Independent Chip Model) is the standard way to convert a chip stack into the real $ value of your position in the tournament, based on how many players are left and how the payouts are structured.
IcmGuide.whyBody: The classic example: you hold half of all the chips in the tournament on the money bubble. That doesn't mean you hold half the prize pool - your real $ equity is noticeably less than half, because busting with half a stack still nets $0, and anyone at the table could still take it down. That's why a call that's profitable in chip terms in a cash game can be a losing call in real money near the bubble or at a final table - that's what people mean by ICM pressure.
IcmGuide.zonesIntro: Exact $ ICM equity is computed from the payout structure and how many players remain - the hand-history file doesn't carry that, so guessing it after the fact wouldn't be honest. What we CAN compute exactly is your stack zone - how many orbits (SB+BB+ante) you can survive without playing a single hand, and what that means for your decisions:
IcmGuide.zoneGreenDesc: Deep - full freedom to play post-flop.
IcmGuide.zoneYellowDesc: Time to tighten ranges and take the pot first more often.
IcmGuide.zoneOrangeDesc: Push-fold kicks in: look for a spot to shove first, there's barely any post-flop play left.
IcmGuide.zoneRedDesc: Straight push-fold - all-in or fold by the chart.
IcmGuide.zoneDeadDesc: Shove any reasonable hand - there's nothing left to wait for.
IcmGuide.bountyTitle: In bounty tournaments, ICM and the bounty pull in opposite directions
IcmGuide.bountyBody: In a regular tournament, ICM almost always pulls toward caution - a risky call near the money bubble costs more than it looks like in chips. Knockout formats (Mystery Bounty, Bounty Hunters and similar on GGPoker) add a counter-force: you're paid separately for taking a villain out, and that reward justifies some calls that pure ICM would talk you out of. The coach sees that a tournament is a bounty format and doesn't judge those calls by the same yardstick as a regular one.
IcmGuide.inProductBody: The hand-history file doesn't show how many players are left in the tournament or how close the money is - that's a limit of the HH format itself, and we don't paper over it with guesses. So the coach doesn't hand you an exact ICM equity in dollars - but it does honestly compute your stack zone on every hand and reminds you: the shorter your stack near the money, the more a risky call actually costs in real money, even when it looks fine in chip terms.
IcmGuide.ctaNote: The first tournament review is free.

LeaksGuide.title: Common leaks in tournament poker at micro stakes
LeaksGuide.intro: A leak isn't a one-off mistake in a single hand - it's a decision you keep making wrong, over and over, without even noticing. One such hand costs almost nothing; a leak that repeats tournament after tournament quietly bleeds more chips over time than any single bad hand ever could.
LeaksGuide.kindsIntro: Every leak is a deviation from one of the reference charts (the same ones on the charts page), not a gut call:
LeaksGuide.openWideDesc: Raise-first-in (RFI) noticeably wider than the reference range for the position.
LeaksGuide.limpDesc: Entering the pot by calling the blind instead of raising - except the small blind heads-up against the big blind, which is a legitimate line.
LeaksGuide.bb3betDesc: 3-betting from the big blind against an open, noticeably wider than the defense chart.
LeaksGuide.shoveDesc: Shoving all-in first into the pot on a short stack, noticeably wider than the push range for the position and depth.
LeaksGuide.vsOpen3betDesc: 3-betting someone else's single open (not from the BB), noticeably wider than the chart.
LeaksGuide.isoDesc: Raising over a limper, noticeably wider than the isolation chart.
LeaksGuide.squeezeDesc: 3-betting over an open and a caller, noticeably wider than the squeeze chart.
LeaksGuide.fourbetDesc: 4-betting after your own open against a 3-bet, noticeably wider than the chart.
LeaksGuide.systematicTitle: One hand isn't a leak yet
LeaksGuide.systematicBody: Opening a bit wide once isn't cause for alarm - could've been situational. Whygrid only calls a leak systemic once it's shown up in at least {minDays} playing days over the last {window} days - at that point it's a pattern, not a coincidence, and worth a closer look.
LeaksGuide.notLuckTitle: A leak isn't the same thing as bad luck
LeaksGuide.notLuckBody: A hand where you played everything right but still lost to an even stronger hand is a cooler, not a leak - the coach doesn't count that as a mistake, even if the chip loss is big. A leak is the opposite: a decision that consistently deviates from the norm, regardless of which card landed on the river. Telling them apart by eye is hard - you're angry at the outcome, not the decision itself. That's why every leak here is counted by the action - opened, entered, shoved wider than the chart - never by the hand's result.
LeaksGuide.inProductBody: In every tournament review, the coach sees not just the single hand but the trend: does this same leak show up on past playing days, or was today the first time it didn't. That shows you not "you made a mistake once" but "this leak has been running for three weeks" - or, just as usefully, that it's already gone.

LeaksGuide.ctaNote: Want to see your own leak trend across tournaments? The first review is free.

GgpokerGuide.title: GGPoker tournament strategy at micro stakes
GgpokerGuide.intro: GGPoker is one of the largest poker platforms in the world, and for micro-stakes players it's one of the most accessible entry points into tournament poker. Whygrid was built with exactly this player in mind: the algorithm reads GGPoker hand-history files natively, the format is detected automatically.
GgpokerGuide.whyMicroBody: Micro-stakes tournaments tend to run faster and rougher than mid and high stakes. Blind structures climb quickly, stacks get short sooner than you'd like, and "shove or wait" decisions come up more often than at deep tables. That's exactly why we have a dedicated reference chart for short-stack play.
GgpokerGuide.formatsTitle: Bounty tournaments run on different math
GgpokerGuide.formatsBody: Micro-stakes GGPoker constantly runs bounty formats - Mystery Bounty, Bounty Hunters, GGMasters KO: every knockout pays a cash reward on top of the placement prize. That changes hand math - calling a short stack's all-in is more profitable than in a regular tournament, because the bounty on their head subsidizes the risk. The coach doesn't mix up a bounty tournament with a regular one: the format is detected from the tournament name in the hand-history file ("Mystery Bounty", "Bounty Hunters", "PKO" and similar), and short-stack reviews account for it separately.
GgpokerGuide.icmLinkText: How a bounty argues with regular tournament math -
GgpokerGuide.parseTitle: How Whygrid reviews your GGPoker tournaments
GgpokerGuide.parseBody: Upload the tournament's hand-history file - the GGPoker format is detected automatically, nothing to pick manually. From there it's like any other room: the algorithm computes exact numbers for every decision, and the coach leads with questions instead of a ready-made verdict.

GgpokerGuide.ctaNote: The first GGPoker tournament review is free.

Landing.alternativesTitle: Why this beats the usual ways
Landing.alternativesSubtitle: Poker mistakes get fixed by review. The only question is which kind.
Landing.altConsultationDescription: About $50 for a single review. Reviewing every tournament that way works out neither on money nor on the coach's time.
Landing.altSelfDescription: You might misread a spot, never find the answer, or mistake someone else's leak for a rule - cementing the mistake instead of fixing it.
Landing.altWhygridDescription: Your own hands. The algorithm does the math exactly, and the coach leads with questions - until you see where you spilled chips yourself.
Landing.benefitNumbersDescription: VPIP, chip losses, position - computed by a deterministic algorithm. The numbers are always right; the AI never makes them up.
Landing.benefitMethodTitle: A question, not a ready answer
Landing.benefitMethodDescription: You're led to the solution with Socratic questions - you see the mistake and remember it yourself, instead of cramming someone else's tip.
Landing.benefitGameDescription: Not abstract textbook spots, but the exact hands you played yourself.
Landing.step1Description: Sign up and drop in a tournament hand-history file from any major poker room - the first one is reviewed free. The algorithm walks through every hand.
Landing.step2Description: On a couple of the most debatable hands, the coach asks why you played it that way - before giving any verdict.
Landing.step3Description: Compare your answer with the review - and see for yourself where your logic didn't match what happened at the table.
Landing.basisTitle: What the review is based on
Landing.basisNumbersDescription: Equity, pot odds, outs, bet sizes, chip losses - all computed by a deterministic algorithm from your file. The same spot always gives the same number. The AI doesn't invent or recompute them - it only explains.
Landing.basisChartsDescription: Opens are checked against charts - an average of the author's working charts and public MTT sources, not the model's guesswork. Not a GTO solver, but a working baseline for online tournaments. Nothing is hidden - the reference charts are open.
Landing.basisCoachDescription: The AI leads with 'why did you play it this way', tests your logic against the numbers, and when unsure honestly asks about the opponent - instead of a blunt verdict. It computes nothing: the numbers are ready before it.
Landing.basisAudience: For the tournament (MTT) player - someone who plays regularly, isn't about to pay for an hour with a coach, but wants every tournament reviewed on their own hands rather than textbook examples.
Landing.objectionExpensiveAnswer: Cheaper than a single coaching session. One pot you don't spill over the long run pays for a month of the subscription.
Landing.objectionDoubtAnswer: Don't take our word for it. Upload your tournament - the first review is free, and judge by your own hands.
Landing.objectionSelfAnswer: You know the theory. The question is whether you see your recurring leaks across dozens of tournaments - that's exactly what the review shows.
Landing.finalSubtitle: The first tournament review is free. Upload your hand-history file - and see for yourself where you lose chips while the coach leads you with questions.

exportIntro.ggpoker: GGPoker doesn't keep a hand-history folder on your computer - everything lives inside PokerCraft, the built-in stats tool in the client. There's no "download everything at once" button either: if you played different formats (tournaments, Spin & Gold), download each section separately.
exportIntro.pokerstars: PokerStars doesn't save hand histories by default - you turn it on once in the client settings. After that, files pile up in a folder on their own, nothing to download manually.
exportIntro.pokerplanets: PokerPlanets is the successor to PokerStars Sochi, so hands are written in the same format as PokerStars, and Whygrid reads them the same way. The room is relatively new - if a settings section is named slightly differently than described below, let us know and we'll fix it.
exportIntro.winamax: In the new Winamax client, history saves to disk automatically, no checkbox required - you just need to find the folder. The old client needs it turned on manually.
exportIntro.888poker: 888poker saves hand history to its own folder under Documents - nothing to turn on, files pile up automatically as you play.
exportIntro.acr: ACR, PokerKing and Black Chip Poker all run on the same WPN (Winning Poker Network) - whichever skin you play, the hand-history files live at the same path.
exportIntro.ipoker: Red Star, Betfair and Betsson are different brands on the same iPoker network - any of its skins works. Important: the client needs to be set to English, or the history may not save correctly.
exportIntro.chico: BetOnline, TigerGaming and SportsBetting all run on the Chico network - you pick the hand-history folder yourself in the client settings the first time you turn it on.

networkLabels.ipoker: iPoker network - any of its skins works

notes.ggpoker: GGPoker has no "download everything at once" button. If you played different formats (tournaments, Spin & Gold), go through each section on the left separately.
notes.pokerstars: Want to see the hand right at the table - enable "Instant Hand History" in the table menu ("Table"). The history language doesn't matter, we read any.
notes.winamax: In the new client the history is saved to disk automatically - no checkbox needed. The old client has one: User Settings → Game settings → "Save My Hand History". Windows hides the AppData folder - in Explorer turn on "Show hidden items" (the "View" tab), otherwise you won't find it.
notes.ipoker: The client must be in English - otherwise the history might not save correctly. Windows hides the AppData folder - turn on showing hidden items.
notes.chico: If some file isn't recognized - let us know and we'll fix it.
notes.pokerplanets: PokerPlanets is the former PokerStars Sochi, so the hands are in PokerStars format and we read them. The room is new, so the settings section may be named a bit differently - if a file isn't recognized, let us know.

pokerstars: The path is shown in "Where To Save" in the same settings
chico: the folder you set in the history settings
pokerplanets: the folder you set in the client's hand-history settings

ggpoker: Open the GGPoker client and sign in.
At the top of the window find the history icon (a list/clock symbol) and click it - a panel of recent events opens.
At the bottom of that panel click "PokerCraft…" - it's the analytics built into the client.
In the PokerCraft window pick "Tournament" in the left menu - the list of tournaments you played appears.
At the top, in the "Date" filter, set a period (e.g. "Last 7 days") and click the red "SHOW" button.
To the left of a tournament tick the checkbox (the checkbox at the column header selects all of them at once).
Click the RED "Setup - game histories" button. The green "Game results" next to it is only the summary, not the hands - it won't work.
A file downloads. If it's an archive (.zip) - unpack it, the .txt files are inside. Upload those to us.
pokerstars: Open the PokerStars client and sign in.
On the left pick "Playing History" → "Hand History".
Tick "Save My Hand History" - without it the files aren't written.
Right there, the "Where To Save" field shows the folder with the files. Note it down (or click "Change Folder" and pick a convenient one).
Open that folder on your computer and grab the tournament .txt files you need.
winamax: Open the Winamax client and sign in.
In the top-left corner click the menu button (three bars).
In the list on the left open the "Tracker" section - the "Hand history file location" row shows the folder with your hand history. The "Open" button opens it.
Grab the tournament .txt files from that folder.
888poker: Open the 888poker client (lobby) and sign in.
Tick "Keep my hand history in" - save the hand history.
The folder is shown next to it (to change it - the "Change Folder" button). Note the path.
Open that folder and grab the tournament .txt files.
acr: Open the client (Americas Cardroom or PokerKing) and sign in.
Click the settings gear in the top-right corner → "Hand Histories" in the left menu. Another way: "Game Info" at the top → "View Hand History" → the "Options" button at the bottom.
Look at the "Destination folder" field - that's the folder with the files.
Open that folder and grab the .txt files.
ipoker: Open the Red Star Poker client (or another iPoker room) and sign in.
In the lobby open "My Account" → "Settings" → the "General" section.
Open the folder with the files (path below; the client name in the path is your room).
Grab the hand-history files - they're .xml or .txt.
chico: Open the BetOnline client (or TigerGaming / SportsBetting) and sign in.
In the lobby, bottom left, open "Settings" → "More options".
In the "History" section enable "Save Hand History" and set the folder to save the hands to.
Play - the .txt files land in that folder. Open it and grab the ones you need.
pokerplanets: Open the PokerPlanets client on your computer and sign in.
Go to the client settings - usually a gear icon or a menu item in the lobby.
Find the hand-history section (Hand History / Playing History) and turn on saving history to your computer.
The folder where the client saves the files is shown right there - note it down (or set your own).
Open that folder and grab the tournament .txt files.

Glossary.helpLabel: What the terms and labels mean
Glossary.title: What the terms mean
Glossary.srDescription: Explanation of metrics, poker terms and our labels
Glossary.vpipDesc: How often you voluntarily enter the pot preflop - by calling or raising (blinds don't count). A rough measure of how loose you play: high means many hands, low means tight.
Glossary.pfrDesc: How often you enter the pot by raising preflop. The gap between VPIP and PFR shows how much you just call instead of applying pressure with a raise.
Glossary.rfiDesc: Opening with a raise when no one has entered the pot before you. The "opener" is exactly this RFI. Each position has its own normal opening range.
Glossary.sprDesc: The ratio of the effective stack to the pot on the flop. A small SPR means the pot is already big relative to stacks, so it's easier to commit; a big one leaves room to maneuver.
Glossary.bbDesc: Stack and hand result are measured in big blinds: "15 BB" is clearer than "383,304 chips" because it doesn't depend on the blind level.
Glossary.afDesc: How many aggressive actions after the flop (bet, raise) you make per passive one (call). Higher means you play the hand more aggressively.
Glossary.potOddsDesc: How much you have to put in relative to what's already in the pot. You compare it with your chances to improve to decide whether the call is profitable.
Glossary.impliedDesc: Future odds: how much more you can win on later streets if your draw hits. A call without direct pot odds can still be right if he pays off your stack when you get there.
Glossary.equityDesc: Your share of the pot - your chance to win the hand right now against a hand or range, as a percent. 60% equity means on average you win 6 of 10.
Glossary.foldEquityDesc: The part of a bet's value that comes from the opponent folding. Even a weak hand can bet profitably if you make him fold often enough.
Glossary.threeBetDesc: A 3-bet is a raise over someone's raise (the open). A 4-bet raises over a 3-bet. Count from the first raise: open, 3-bet, 4-bet, 5-bet.
Glossary.limpDesc: Entering the pot by just calling the blind instead of raising. Almost always a leak: no initiative, and you let the table in cheap. Exception - the small blind heads-up vs the big blind.
Glossary.isoDesc: Raising over a limper to push everyone else out and play him heads-up, in position, with the initiative.
Glossary.restealDesc: A 3-bet all-in on a short stack (about 10-25 BB) over someone's open. You either take the pot now or get it in with live equity.
Glossary.donkDesc: Betting into the previous street's aggressor before he acts. From an amateur it's usually a real hand; from a reg it's often a bluff.
Glossary.checkRaiseDesc: Check first, then raise after the opponent bets. When it lands on you (especially on the turn) it's usually strength - default fold unless you have a read.
Glossary.allinDesc: Betting your whole stack. When it comes at you there are no more bets - the decision is just your equity vs his range against the price to call.
Glossary.pushFoldDesc: Short-stack mode (roughly 15 BB and below): all-in or fold by fixed Nash charts, no regular postflop play.
Glossary.drawDesc: A draw is an unmade hand (flush or straight draw) that needs a card. Outs are cards that improve you; clean outs give you the BEST hand, not the second-best. Lean on the clean ones.
Glossary.topPairDesc: Top pair pairs the highest board card. An overpair is a pocket pair above the whole board (e.g. KK on Q-7-2).
Glossary.blockersDesc: Cards in your hand that cut down the opponent's strong combos. An ace in your hand blocks his AA and AK - so you run into strength less often.
Glossary.polarDesc: A range of two extremes - either very strong hands or bluffs, nothing in between. A big bet at you is often polarized: a monster or a bluff, with medium hands behind.
Glossary.wetBoardDesc: A board with lots of draws - suited, connected cards (like 9-8-7 or two of a suit). Flushes and straights get there easily: you value-bet bigger, but there's more danger.
Glossary.coolerDesc: A hand where you played it right but lost - a strong hand ran into an even stronger one. Not a mistake, just variance; the coach doesn't score it against you.
Glossary.icmDesc: In a tournament chips aren't equal to money: near a bust-out or the money bubble, risk costs more than in cash. Be more careful in marginal spots where busting is expensive. Amateurs don't think about ICM.
Glossary.bountyDesc: A reward for knocking a player out in a knockout tournament. Calling off a short stack's head is subsidized by the bounty - the real threshold is below normal pot odds.
Glossary.criticalDesc: The most decisive hand of the tournament - the coach leads the review and asks "why". It often lands here by the run-out, so a big loss here isn't necessarily a mistake.
Glossary.matchDesc: When the algorithm sees the mistake in this hand is the same one you've repeated over your history. The coach then points out it's a pattern, not a one-off.
Glossary.passedDesc: A marker for a tournament where you reached the verdict on the hands worth discussing. The main work is done; the tail of strong and medium hands is optional.
Glossary.orientirDesc: Your mark of how deeply you understand poker. The coach uses it to tune how much to explain - for your first tournaments. After that it goes by your actual hands.
Glossary.chartsDesc: Mirrors of your preflop decisions (opens, BB defense, vs open, isolation, push-fold) against reference ranges - where you're wider or tighter than standard.
Glossary.startHereDesc: The top slot on the tournament page - your entry point: the most questionable unreviewed hand worth discussing to start with.

ReferenceCharts.bvbIntro: Everyone folded, the small blind open-raised - how to defend the BB. The widest defence in the game: the SB opens very wide.
ReferenceCharts.restealIntro: Someone opened and you are short - which hands to jam. Pick the opener's position and your stack.
ReferenceCharts.restealLegendWeight: Jam at a weight - allowed, not mandatory; the coach won't scold it
ReferenceCharts.cvpIntro: Someone open-shoved with up to 14 BB - what to call with. Pick the pusher's position and stack. Live stacks behind make the call slightly tighter.
ReferenceCharts.cvrIntro: You opened and got 3-bet jammed for 10-25 BB - what continues. Against a late open they rejam wide, against an early one - tight and strong.
ReferenceCharts.cvrLegendFold: Fold - open-and-fold versus a jam is fine, don't chase 2 BB
ReferenceCharts.fourbetIntro: You opened and got 3-bet - which hands to 4-bet. Calling the 3-bet is not judged by this chart: it's a stack-depth decision.
ReferenceCharts.fourbetLegendBluff: 4-bet bluff with a blocker - at a weight, optional
ReferenceCharts.fourbetLegendOut: Not a 4-bet - call or fold by the spot
ReferenceCharts.squeezeIntro: A 3-bet over an open and a caller. Squeeze width is very spot-dependent, so there is no hard border - the chart only cuts obvious trash that no spot squeezes.
ReferenceCharts.squeezeLegendOut: Obvious trash - not a squeeze from anywhere
ReferenceCharts.legendBorder: Borderline: not a mistake, but not a recommendation - the coach won't flag these
ReferenceCharts.title: Charts
ReferenceCharts.intro: The reference ranges your coach judges your play against. This is the baseline; how you actually open is shown in "Your charts" on "My tournaments".
ReferenceCharts.openIntro: Which hands to open the pot with when everyone folds to you. Pick a position.
ReferenceCharts.sbNote: On the small blind this is the raising range. Weak hands aren't folded when it's folded to you - they limp, a separate legitimate line.
ReferenceCharts.legendAlways: Always open - the core of the range
ReferenceCharts.legendSometimes: Sometimes, depending on the spot (roughly half the time)
ReferenceCharts.disclaimer: This is not GTO solver output - these are your coach's working ranges for micro-stakes tournaments. The core matches solver ranges; in early positions our ranges are softer than the solver's - the coach only punishes clearly loose opens, not borderline hands. Want to play tighter - stick to the solid lime zone. There is no single correct chart: strong players and different schools use their own ranges, and that is fine. We keep ONE consistent reference so the coach never contradicts itself; if you play a different chart, say so in the review - the coach will take it into account instead of calling your hand a mistake.
ReferenceCharts.depthNote: Baseline for stacks of 20 big blinds and deeper: shorter stacks are push-fold territory. Deeper than 60 blinds the edges can widen slightly.
ReferenceCharts.pushIntro: Which hands to go all-in with first when everyone folds to you. Pick a stack and a position.
ReferenceCharts.pushLegendAlways: Push - the hand is in the all-in range
ReferenceCharts.pushDisclaimer: These ranges are taken from Nash push-fold charts and checked against public ones: this spot is solved math, there are no solver disagreements here. From 15 blinds push-fold no longer applies - that's regular opening territory (chart above). HJ plays the CO chart.
ReferenceCharts.bbIntro: How to respond from the BB to a single open of about 2.5 blinds. Pick the opener's position - the later it is, the wider the defense.
ReferenceCharts.bbLegendThreebetBluff: 3-bet bluff at a frequency - allowed, not required; the coach won't flag it
ReferenceCharts.bbLegendCallSometimes: Call sometimes, depending on the spot
ReferenceCharts.bbDisclaimer: An average of solver charts and a practical micro-stakes baseline: thin solver "junk" at the calling edges is trimmed - it doesn't make money against weak fields. The coach only flags 3-bets clearly wider than this boundary. Defense against a small-blind open is a different spot and isn't judged by this chart.
ReferenceCharts.vsOpenTitle: 3-betting vs an open (not from the BB)
ReferenceCharts.vsOpenIntro: Which hands to 3-bet a single open with when you're not in the big blind. Pick your position.
ReferenceCharts.vsOpenLegendOut: 3-bet not recommended: call or fold depending on the spot
ReferenceCharts.vsOpenDisclaimer: The most nuanced preflop spot, so the chart only judges the 3-bet: cold calling is deliberately not graded - it depends heavily on position, opponent and depth. The coach only flags 3-bets clearly wider than the boundary.
ReferenceCharts.isoIntro: Which hands to isolate a limper with. Pick your position.
ReferenceCharts.isoLegendOverlimp: Small pair: overlimp - isolating with it counts as a mistake
ReferenceCharts.isoDisclaimer: Isolation is almost the opening range, but slightly tighter: small pairs 22-66 are better off just limping along (set-mining cheaply), and the junky bottom folds. Against several limpers or with a big sizing isolate even tighter.
ReferenceCharts.ctaText: That's the baseline. Upload your hand histories - the algorithm will compare your game against these very charts for free and build your personal charts: where you're wider than the norm and where you're tighter. No subscription needed.
ReferenceCharts.sbLimpIntro: Folded to you, you are in the small blind. Strong hands open with a raise, the rest come in limping - half a blind is already invested and a cheap flop against one opponent pays off. The grid answers the second question: what to do when the big blind raises your limp.
ReferenceCharts.sbLimpLegendRaise: Open with a RAISE - limping this hand is not our line
ReferenceCharts.sbLimpLegendCall: Limp and CALL the big blind raise
ReferenceCharts.sbLimpLegendFold: Limp, but fold to a raise
ReferenceCharts.sbLimpDisclaimer: Defence against a raise over your limp is wider than usual here, and that is deliberate: opponents know that limping means seeing a cheap flop, so they attack limps widely - including with trash. Against that, an ace, king, broadway or a suited hand already calls. Limp-raising is NOT part of the reference: it is a situational play based on reading the opponent (works against an aggressive regular, pointless against a passive one), so the coach never treats its absence as a mistake.
ReferenceCharts.relatedIntro: The charts show what to do. Here's the spots and terms explained on their own, apart from the numbers: ranges, ICM, leaks, how a review actually works.

ReferenceCharts.relatedIcmCta: What is ICM in poker tournaments
ReferenceCharts.relatedLeaksCta: Common leaks in tournament poker at micro stakes
ReferenceCharts.relatedHandReviewCta: How a poker hand review actually works
